subsystems.name: Polynomial arithmetic core
subsystems.role: Performs the number-theoretic transform (NTT) and modular multiplication that dominate lattice-based cryptography.

subsystems.name: Sampler and random number generator
subsystems.role: Generates the random noise and secret polynomials that give lattice schemes their security.
parts: sampling logic (e.g., centered binomial, rejection sampling)

subsystems.name: Memory and key storage
subsystems.role: Holds keys, polynomials, and intermediate results during computation.

subsystems.name: Control and interface
subsystems.role: Sequences operations and connects the accelerator to the host system.

subsystems.name: Side-channel protection
subsystems.role: Makes the hardware resistant to timing, power, and electromagnetic attacks.

buildSteps.title: Select algorithms and parameters
buildSteps.detail: Choose the standardized schemes to support — for example the NIST lattice-based key encapsulation and signature algorithms — and fix the parameter sets (e.g., security levels).

buildSteps.title: Design microarchitecture
buildSteps.detail: Decide how to split work between hardware and software: dedicated NTT cores, samplers, and memory buffers, and how they pipeline.

buildSteps.title: Write and verify RTL
buildSteps.detail: Implement the design in a hardware description language (Verilog or VHDL) and verify it against reference software models using simulation and formal methods.

buildSteps.title: Synthesize and place-and-route
buildSteps.detail: Use EDA tools to map the RTL to a target process node (e.g., 7 nm or 28 nm), optimizing for area, power, and speed.

buildSteps.title: Tape-out and fabricate
buildSteps.detail: Send the final layout to a semiconductor foundry for fabrication. This is a major cost and only justified for high-volume or high-performance applications.

buildSteps.title: Package and test
buildSteps.detail: Assemble the die into a package, then test for functionality, performance, and side-channel leakage.

buildSteps.title: Develop drivers and integration
buildSteps.detail: Write software drivers, cryptographic libraries, and APIs so the accelerator works with TLS, VPNs, and other protocols.

prerequisites.why: NIST finalized the first lattice-based standards in 2024, giving hardware designers a stable target.
The number-theoretic transform is well understood and widely used in software and hardware.

prerequisites.tech: Hardware description languages and EDA tools
prerequisites.why: Standard tools for designing and verifying digital logic.
Masking and constant-time methods are known but costly and not fully standardized for PQC.
Needed to protect keys and generate randomness; available in commercial secure elements.

pathway.milestone: FPGA and academic ASIC prototypes demonstrate lattice-based accelerators.
pathway.unlocks: Proof that PQC can run at line speed with acceptable area and power.

pathway.milestone: Commercial ASIC accelerators appear in network interface cards, hardware security modules, and smart cards.
pathway.unlocks: Offload of PQC from general-purpose CPUs, enabling high-throughput secure communications.

pathway.milestone: Integration into mainstream TLS libraries and network protocols (e.g., TLS 1.3, IPsec).
pathway.unlocks: Widespread adoption without replacing existing infrastructure.

pathway.milestone: Accelerators become standard in cloud servers, IoT devices, and consumer electronics. Isogeny-based schemes remain at research stage due to broken candidates.
pathway.unlocks: Quantum-resistant security everywhere, from data centres to embedded sensors.
